8 Nov 2012 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 6469
Second Reading
Hon DAVID CARTER (Minister for Primary Industries)  on behalf of the

items.speaker: Minister of Science and Innovation
items.text: I move, That the Advanced Technology Institute
Bill be now read a second time . The bill establishes a new Crown entity, the Advanced
Technology Institute—also known as ATI—a new high-tech HQ to support innovative
New Zealand businesses primarily in the manufacturing and services sector. The
purpose of the Advanced Technology Institute is simple: to help get New Zealand’s best
ideas out of the lab and into the market place more quickly. Kiwis are great at coming
up with smart ideas, but we need to become  more successful at translating those ideas
more quickly into commercially successf ul products. The Advanced Technology
Institute will help increase the number of re search and development - capable firms, lift
New Zealand’s exports of high-value manufactured goods and services, and support the
Government’s aspirations around economic gr owth. It will focus on industries with
high-growth potential, such as the food and beverage manufacturing sectors, the
agritechnology sectors, digital technologies , health technology, therapeutics, and high-
value wood products.
When the Advanced Technology Institute Bill was referred to the Education and
Science Committee, the House requested that  it be reported back by 6 November in
order for the Advanced Technology Instit ute to be up and running in early 2013. The
committee, in fact, reported back on 23 October,  and I am grateful to the chair and the
members for their prompt consideration of this legislation. Submissions on the bill were
highly supportive of the Government’s ambitions for the Advanced Technology
Institute. Useful information was provided on how submitters saw the Advanced
Technology Institute op erating within the research a nd development sector and how it
could operate to minimise perceived negative effects. The Government shares the views
of many submitters that collaboration will be the key to the success of the Advanced
Technology Institute. No single institution can expect to maintain all of the research
capability required to service the manufacturing and services sector. To succeed,
therefore, the Advanced Technology Institute must work with Crown research institutes,
with the universities and polytechs, and wi th other research pr oviders to develop
partnerships that maximise commercialis ation opportunities, an d to ensure that
businesses better utilise existing research and development capabilities.
To underline the importance of those objecti ves, the bill’s operating principles
mandating collaboration have been strengthened. I am aware that the committee heard a
number of submissions regarding the nature and the extent of the Advanced Technology
Institute’s in-house research  capability. It was always intended that the Advanced
Technology Institute would look to harness ca pability that exists  across all research
institutions, and that it woul d not seek to unnecessarily du plicate expertise elsewhere.
That said, Industrial Research Ltd current ly undertakes a significant research and
development programme, and it will become pa rt of the Advanced Technology Institute
upon its establishment. The Advanced Technology Institute board will decide the mix of
resources and capability it requires to deliver its functions, and this will naturally evolve
over time. The bill simply provides the Advanced Technology Institute with the
function of undertaking research and development. It is not pr escriptive as to the extent
or form.
A number of submitters requested that membership of the board of the Advanced
Technology Institute or the stakeholder advi sory group be prescribed to those with
characteristics such as geographical or profe ssional representation, institutional type, or
unions. The board’s appointment is governed by the Cabinet circular outlining the
6470 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 8 Nov 2012
process for increasing diversity of board me mbership, while the Minister must consult
with the board before esta blishing the advisory group, pr oviding the means to identify
specialist areas of assistance. The potential area of conflict of the institute being both a
funder of business research and developmen t grants and a research and development
provider has always been recogni sed. This bill requires that  systems and procedures are
put in place to ensure that the Adva nced Technology Institute acts fairly and
transparently in allocating and administering research and development funding. I am
confident those systems and pr ocedures will be robust and will withstand scrutiny. The
Advanced Technology Institute must also re port on its implementation in its annual
report, as must the Auditor-General as part of the annual financial audit process.
The Advanced Technology Institute, which is  to be named after the late Sir Paul
Callaghan, forms part of this Government’s  commitment to promoting science and
innovation in New Zealand through the Busine ss Growth Agenda. In recent months we
have announced a number of in itiatives to improve linkages between science, business,
and innovation. These include making improvements to business incubator settings,
assessing whether the tax treatment is discouraging firms from research and
development expenditure, promoting co-f unding to encourage business innovation,
improving the economic contribution of both universities and polytechnics, better
monitoring of public science investment, a nd incentivising public research institutions.
Increasing business innovation is key to growin g the economy. It is key to creating jobs
and key to raising the living standards of a ll New Zealanders. This Government has set
the goal of raising the amount businesses spend on research and development from
where it is currently, at 0.45 percent, to 1 percent of GDP.
The success of the Advanced Technology Institute will be measured in many ways,
but one of the most important will be how much it helps manufacturing and services
firms to innovate, to increas e productivity, to grow exports, and to operate more
efficiently. The Advanced Technology Instit ute Bill strikes a balance between being
flexible enough for the Advanced Technology In stitute to determine which services and
activities will best support fi rms in the manufacturing and se rvices sector to innovate,
and to commercialise their products, while also being clear about the institute’s purpose,
the scope of its functions, and the operating pr inciples by which it is expected to abide.
The Advanced Technology Inst itute will help ensure that  innovative Kiwi firms have
access to the necessary skills, facilities, infr astructure, and new technologies that they
need to lift their competitiveness and, in turn, boost New Zealand’s economic growth. I
commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: I would like to acknowledge the
Minister who has just resume d his seat, the Hon David Cart er, and I wish him well in
his bid for Speaker, Mr Assistant Speaker . I also acknowledge the late Sir Paul
Callaghan, a very distinguished sc ientist and author of the book Wool to Weta , and a
passionate advocate of a high- tech strategy for the New Ze aland economy. I note that
we are a long way from the noble aspirations that Sir Paul has left us with.
The Advanced Technology Institute Bill w ill make a very small but, unfortunately,
insignificant contribution to that goal. Labour is supporting th e bill because it would be
inappropriate not to, but I wish to comment in these remarks on the great gap that will
remain between the Government’s rhetoric and the strategy that its policies are
employing.
Just in the last week we are reminded ag ain of that gap. Haier bought out Fisher and
Paykel Appliances, and we stand to lose, I think, the country’s second-largest provider
of patents to overseas deployment and ownership. Hillside railway workshops has again
been in the news, with the chief executive of  Farra Engineering criticising the failure of
the Government’s policy mix to reflect the ove rall interests of the region’s engineering
8 Nov 2012 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 6471
and manufacturing sector in the State-ow ned enterprises’ decision making. Today the
Government has presided over the furthe r watering down of the emissions trading
scheme to reduce the incentives for sm art, clean technology. Dynamic Controls
announced a downsizing of its Canterbury plant, and unemployment—here is the
kicker—hit 7.3 percent, agains t projections of a decline. It actually went up by a
massive 0.6 percent, which is the worst since Bill English was last the Minister of
Finance in 1999. Why is this ha ppening? I guess the key point is it is not an accident. It
is the logical, necessary out growth of a fundamentally fl awed strategic framework,
which this bill does not change.
What did Government members think woul d happen when they have a tax system
that favours speculation over high-tech, wh ich has no capital gains regime—we are
almost alone in the Western World in that—no research and development tax credit, and
no accelerated depreciation for high techno logy? What did they think would happen
with an insufficient savings regime that  starves local business and high-tech of
investment capital and makes them overly reliant on imported overseas capital and the
sell-out of ownership, whic h that too often, too young, too frequently requires? What
did they think would happen if they continue d to subsidise pastoral agriculture by not
bringing it into the emissions trading scheme , and providing irrigation subsidies while
starving industrial and manuf acturing industries of the inve stment capital and the fair
opportunities that they need?
We have a perpetual bias in our economic framework that is seeing farms and banks
do OK—banks do more than OK—but is seei ng industry, high-tech, and manufacturing
sliding to what looks like an eventual demise. In the meantime we are exploiting
mineral and petroleum resources through foreign-owned multinationals, through which
we claim too little in royalties and through which we will lose control of our underlying
resources. The Government is failing to pr ovide appropriate market signals to State-
owned enterprises like Hillside railway workshops in Dunedin, and is instead dressing
them for sale. The Government is running a 20 th century monetary policy framework
during a 21st century global financial crisis, an d wondering why our exchange rate and
interest rates are too high and our current account deficit is overtaking that of Greece, to
become the worst in the developed world.
These are not accidental consequences. Thes e are the logical, the predictable, the
necessary, and the scientific ally proven results of a fundamentally flawed economic
framework. What do we get? We get high unemployment, a world record current
account deficit, and manufacturing and high-te ch in crisis. “What to do?”, says the
Government. “How will we dress this up?”, sa ys the spin doctor. Well, National is too
locked into its low-tech, dumb-developmen t strategy to change that. Its political
constituencies and its own rhetoric will not allow it to make that change, and what it
desperately wants to avoid is for the public to get the idea that to  change the strategy,
they first have to change the Government —to change the strategy, they change the
Government.
This side of the House will rise to that historic responsibility, because that side of the
House not only will not but cannot. So it came up with the followi ng plan. In Budget
2012 it would cut Vote Economic Development by something like $130 million, and it
would reinvest about one-third of it in the Advanced Technology Institute, and it would
have the Advanced Technology Institute Bill, which it would then trumpet as the
solution to the decline of high-tech.
Well, I am a former director of Industrial  Research Ltd, the current name of that
body before the Government invokes the name of  the late and great Sir Paul Callaghan,
and a director of the current body said to me: “The bill is flaw ed.” Why? “Because
companies”, he said, “are best placed to understand their own technology needs. What
6472 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 8 Nov 2012
they need is more support around finance a nd marketing and internationalisation, and
this bill will not help the commercialisation process.”

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: Nothing to do with a whiff of personal interest?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: No personal interest in that—no personal interest in that.
That is scraping the barrel, Mr Simpson—scraping the barrel. So if a fig leaf is required,
that is this bill.
Labour supports the bill. Might  the public be surprised? Well, I suppose a fig leaf is
better than no leaf, and thro wing a few crumbs at manufac turing is about all this
Government is capable of. We will take the crumbs, and then when we are elected in 2
years’ time we will have a decent strategic framework and a proper policy mix as well.
Then we will see unemployment come down. Then we will see exports go up. Then we
will see hope in the eyes of young New Zeala nders, especially young science graduates.
Then we will see a decline in the queues to the departure gates for Kiwis whose dream
has faded, whose future is fading, and whose commitment to the current Government
has gone.
One thing that cheers me up is that the polls are not lying—this Government’s hold
on New Zealand is weakening, day by day, week by week, and month by month. The
right track / wrong track has cros sed over and the left bloc is  ahead of the right bloc on
most polls, and change is coming. Change is coming—it just cannot come soon enough.
It cannot come soon enough for the high-tech firms. It cannot come soon enough for the
Dunedin manufacturing cluster. It cannot come soon enough for the 7.3 percent of New
Zealanders on the unemployment scrap heap—oh, they have gone quiet now. Where are
the Weet-Bix now, National backbench? Let me say it again—7.3 percent. Budget 2011
said it would be 5 percent by now, but it went up, not do wn. It did not go from 6.7
percent to 6.6 percent; it went up from 6.7 percent to 7.3 percent.
It is a catastrophe, and it is  a predictable catastrophe. It is the logical outgrowth of a
flawed strategic framework and policies that  are not worth the pa per the glossies are
written on. And Steven Joyce fiddles while Ro me burns. Steven Joyce’s main claim to
fame is pumping out glossy papers to repeat  projects that were done  in yesteryear, and
now there is this fig leaf for the science community.
What the science community is saying to the Labour Opposition is: “Get a real plan,
guys. Sure, we will take ATI, that is fine, but get a real plan.” New Zealand’s future
does not lie in chopping down and exporting ra w logs. It does not lie just in milking
more cows. Sir Paul Callaghan was a great  man, and his vision was from wool to
Weta—from wool to digita l technology. It was not subs idies for polluters and
borrowing to pay for it. It was not locking in the i ndustries of yesteryear with a flawed
monetary policy and a flawed tax framework. O h, yeah, we will take  this bill, but we
want a whole lot more besides.

items.speaker: NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am very pleased to speak on the
Advanced Technology Institute Bill. Can I start by acknowledging the late Sir Paul
Callaghan. He was a great man, he did have great vision for New Zealand, and this
legislation is actually about delivering on th at vision. But, firstly, can I take just a
moment to comment on the wider economic age nda and the theatrics that we just had
from—I believe it was David Cunliffe, but I think it is interesting that he is filling in for
the actual research and innovati ons spokesperson, who has been  very quiet on this bill,
the leader of the Labour Party, David Shearer . Perhaps this is a very ominous sign.
Perhaps this actually—

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: Ian Shearer?

items.speaker: NIKKI KAYE
items.text: My colleague says “Ian Shearer”. Perhaps the real truth is that we
just heard the leadership speech of the Labour  Party from David Cunliffe. But can I say
that everything that we just heard from David Cunliffe is rhetoric. Whenever it comes to
8 Nov 2012 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 6473
many economic initiatives—and we heard about Weta—when it comes to The Hobbit
films, do those members support these ini tiatives? No, they vot e them down. When it
comes to greater intensification, they vote it down. When it comes to mineral
exploration, they vote it down.
What has been very interesti ng through this legislative proc ess is to see a very clear
comparison between the parties. We are a party that is supporting a framework to enable
businesses to get more ideas to market quicker. This bill was supported by a range of
parties across the House, but the key thing is—and we saw it in the Labour Party
minority report—those members talk the talk, but when it comes to the actual detail we
see them looking after their mates. We saw this with their advocating for union seats on
the Advanced Technology Inst itute Bill. That is extrao rdinary. Their major economic
solution for New Zealand is to hold up our commercialisation vehicle with union seats.
It was a very collaborative process for this bill, and there were many great changes as
a result of the Education and Science Committee’s consid eration. But can I say that
when it came to the crunch, when we saw La bour’s true colours in  the minority report,
we saw a party that is outdated  and back in the 1990s. We sa w a party that is absolutely
beholden to the unions. We saw a party that is committed to legislating for everything.
What I am confident of is that, whether it is the fact that we have increased science
funding by 17 percent, whether it is the fact that we have made major investments in
infrastructure, or whether it is the fact that we are deliveri ng a crucial piece of
legislation that is going to ensure that we have greater collaboration between our
scientists and our businesses, we are actua lly delivering. We have a plan, and we are
investing in that plan by 17 percent additional science funding.
If you compare that with the Labour members, they are very clear that they want to
legislate for their union mates and that they want to stop everything else from
happening in other areas of our economy,  whether it is mineral exploration,
intensification in terms of farming, or labour  laws—all of these things that add up to
having a much more flexible economic agenda  that is actually focused on growth and
jobs. I think we need to mention that, because we constantly hear the rhetoric but we do
not see the detail that will actually take New Zealand forward.
We had a range of submissions on this bill that were incredibly  supportive. I think
there were 23 submissions—seven oral submissions. I also acknowledge that in terms of
the changes made to the bill we strengt hened the clauses around collaboration, and I
want to thank Kiwinet for its submissions on that. I also want to acknowledge other
members of the committee, such as Tracey  Martin, David Clendon, Megan Woods, and
other members of the Labour Party. I think it was an incredibly collaborative process.
Under very tight time frames we achieved a lot in making some ve ry valuable changes
to this bill, whether it was th e collaboration clauses or whether it was ensuring there
was consultation with the wider sector.
I think this is a ve ry good piece of legisl ation. It is part of our wider economic
agenda, which involves not only greater investment in science, which we have delivered
on, and not only ensuring that we have ve ry good economic polic y in terms of our
labour laws, but also ensuring that we have greater collaboration vi a vehicles like this.
The sum of $166 million is an extraordinary am ount to ensure that we have high-tech
centres right across New Zealand, particularly in Auckland and in Canterbury. I am very
confident that through the select committee pr ocess we have delivered a vehicle that
will be crucial in delivering on Sir Paul Callaghan’s vision of ensuring that more
businesses are able to take their ideas to market.
I want to comment on a couple of key clause s such as the net benefit clause. I think
that was a very positive change. We recognised that we wanted to have a similar test to
the Crown research institutes, so we changed that from “net benefit” to “benefit”. As I
6474 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 8 Nov 2012
said before, we made a key change ar ound the collaboration, to  ensure that the
Advanced Technology Institute would not be replicating current and existing funding
structures. Another key point  that was made throughout a number of submissions was
the issue of the research framework and its capability. We were quite clear on this side
of the House that we do not think it is appropriate to be legislating for that detail,
because things do change in a rapidly changing environment in terms of technology.
Also, if a country wants to be flexible about where it spends its money and where its
economic agenda is, we do not want to tie up the institute by being overly prescriptive.
Finally, a number of other points were men tioned in the speech of the Minister for
Primary Industries around the need not to necessarily prescribe the detail around
stakeholders—the stakeholder advisory boar d. I think that was the right thing to do
because, as has been mentioned in Cabinet circulars, there are a number of provisions
around ensuring there is greater geographical representation.
I am very pleased to commend this bill to th e House. I think it will be a key vehicle
for greater commercialisation, taking more New Zealand busi nesses’ ideas to market. I
think it has been a very co llaborative process across the House. I think it was done
under difficult time frames but that we mitigat ed that by ensuring that we wrote to a
range of submitters. It was very pleasing that only a couple of submissions were
opposed to the bill. It is important to note th at this is part of our wider Government
economic agenda, which includes greater inve stment in science, real policies around
infrastructure investment, and good polic ies around labour laws. The Opposition has
raised what I think are very overly prescriptive policies in terms of this bill as part of its
philosophical vision for New Zealand, wh ich is to tie the country up and oppose
everything. I am very pleased to commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: I am very happy to take a call on the
Advanced Technology Institute Bill and to deal with some of what we have heard in the
House this afternoon, because it is simply astounding that members opposite can think
that this legislation is going to deliver on the vision of Sir Paul Callaghan. It is just
astounding. This is a woeful pi ece of legislation that needed streng thening, and it is a
missed opportunity. Labour is supporting this legislation. It is supporting it in a very
lukewarm way. We firmly believe that th is is an opportunity lost. We are very
disappointed that members opposite have faile d to take the opportunity that setting up
something like the Advanced Technology Institute could have afforded us. I think it
speaks volumes that the chair of the Education and Science Committee, Nikki Kaye,
who saw this legislation through, used 3 or 4 minutes of her speech  on this piece of
legislation to take low blows and cheap shot s, instead of addre ssing the substance and
some very real concerns that have been raised in this legislation.
We on this side of the House are fearful that this is yet another grand scheme from a
Government that talks big on science and innovation but has failed to deliver a game-
changer. We are fearful because of its track record. We have real reason to be fearful
here. There is nothing in this legislation that addresses the structural flaws for the
manufacturing sector. It is with some irony that we are standing he re today discussing
and debating a bill that is around more innovation for our high-value manufacturing
sector on a day when we have had une mployment figures out that show the
manufacturing sector is continui ng to bleed jobs. This is what this bill is about. It is
about strengthening this sector, and it is about the creation of high-value jobs and highly
skilled jobs, and this bill will fail to do that.
There are some worrying echoes of other initiatives that this Government has tried.
We can just look to its voucher scheme, whic h has been a complete and utter flop. This
was talked big in Budget 2010. There was going to be $20 million over 4 years to high-
value manufacturing firms, with co-inve stment for projects of over $100,000. Well,
8 Nov 2012 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 6475
what has happened? It has failed to spend this money, because it has no understanding
of what is required for innovation in New Zealand. What have we got in 2012? Well,
less than $4 million has been granted in 2 years, and only one in three of these projects
has been over $100,000. It has had to expand th is into the agritech sector, away from
concentrating just on the high-value manufactur ing sector, and it has had to take the co-
funding option down to $30,000. There are some ve ry worrying parallels with what has
happened with the passage of this Advan ced Technology Institute idea since it was
born.
So what we had from the chair of the se lect committee, Nikki Kaye, was her saying
that there were some very clear comparisons that emerged in the deliberations over this
legislation at the select committee. Well, I ag ree completely with her. There were some
very clear comparisons that emerged betw een the Government and the Opposition side
of the table. What emerged from the Govern ment side of the table was a failure to
understand what 21 st century innovation looks like in New Zealand, and what it will
take to truly transform our economy. We have  heard a whole lot of  hysterical shrieking
that we want to look after our union mate s by daring to suggest that maybe workers
might have some input into innovative processes.
I actually want to take you through what  Labour suggested in terms of the
stakeholder advisory panel. Labour said it would be really good if we had good industry
input into what was happening in the high- value manufacturing se ctor. We noted that
there were very few submissions from indus try because of a rushed process, which I
will come back to later. But we thought a bout the people who were investing their
money, setting up the businesses—we want to ha ve their voice heard. We want them on
the stakeholder advisory panel, and we would quite like the other providers of research,
science, and technology innovation there as well as the universities and the Crown
research institutes. We would like their voi ce heard. And then what about the people
who actually perform the innovation? What about the people who work as scientists, the
people who work as technicians, and the people who work in the manufacturing firms
on the shop floor and on the lines? These peop le have got a pretty good idea about what
innovation takes and how it is that we can transform this. Because you know what? This
is what happens all over the world.
If members opposite knew anything about what 21 st century innovation looks like
and how other countries are doing it and succeeding, they would get past their hysterical
shrieking. We need only look at one of the most effective lobby groups in science in this
country, the Public Service Association scie nce committee, which is made up of some
of the top scientists in this country. But no, they are members of  unions! You certainly
could not have them inputting into anything ! Members opposite need to take off their
blinkers and realise what it will take to tr ansform our manufactur ing industries in New
Zealand. Hearing from everybody with some stake in the game is something that we are
fully supportive of.
We also thought it would be a really good id ea to ensure that there would be some
regional representation on this stakeholder advisory panel. We thought that it would be
really good if the areas where the economic development potential resided and existed
were represented so that we could get a broa d view of what innovati on in this sector in
New Zealand might look like. But no, we could not have anything like that! Labour will
be putting up a number of amendments that address these representation issues. We will
be putting up a number of amendments for this bill, because actually we want to see this
succeed.
What we are really disappointed by is the f act that this Government simply does not
understand what it is going to take. For us, i nnovation is a means to an end. It is about
good regional and economic development that will create jobs, and higher-paying jobs,
6476 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 8 Nov 2012
which is clearly something that this Government does not turn its mind to, when we
look at the employment figures that came out today. Actually, j obs do not happen by
magic. They take a Government that is wil ling to take an interest, and a Government
that is willing to invest. We think that the Advanced Technology Institute could actually
afford us such an opportunity, but this is a Government that is not willing to even
countenance that we may have a look at that.
What we believe is that innovation in Ne w Zealand needs to be an interconnected
and joined-up process, and that we need to have industry, we need to have the science
providers, and we need to understand what it takes to commercialise. We have a number
of concerns with this bill, and not only a bout the representation. We  have a worry that
the Advanced Technology Institute is going to succeed or fail on its ability to be part of
this interconnected and joined-up group of people. It is going to rise and fall on its
ability to be an active player. The way that this Government is setting this institute up is
ensuring and is embedding—through this very permissive enabling legislation—that it
is going to be seen as a competitor to be feared.
Members on the Government side of the H ouse will not even c ountenance that we
put in some protections to make sure that it is seen as an organisation that does not
unnecessarily replicate and duplicate functions  that are already successfully being
carried out. They simply would not countenan ce that we would put those protections in
place. Nor would they even agree to the fact that the idea that this new organisation is
both a funder and a provider might create a li ttle bit of suspicion amongst other people
with whom it is going to have to go out there and form very  strong collaborations. It is
its ability to colla borate and its ability to work not  only with industry but with other
providers that will make this an institute that will succeed or fail.
Labour also sees the Advanced Technology Institute as something that needs to be
part of a wider economic development st rategy. Labour thinks that the Advanced
Technology Institute cannot succ eed unless it also has a rese arch and development tax
credit sitting alongside it. We heard from one submitter, the Manufacturers and
Exporters Association—in fact, one of the few industry subm issions that we received—
that it saw that the tax credit was a fundame ntal thing that needed to be addressed for
manufacturing to succeed in this country. We also hear d from the Manufacturers and
Exporters Association that one of the biggest impediment s to it being able to innovate,
to it being able to hire, a nd to it being able to grow was the vol atility of the New
Zealand dollar, and that it was about time that we had a Government that was willing to
address the macroeconomic issues that we re undermining the manufacturing sector’s
ability to get on to succeed in this country.
The Advanced Technology Institute cannot exist in isolation. I hope members
opposite will consider at futu re readings the amendments that Labour put up, because
we want to see this succeed, but we are fearfu l that in its present form it will not. Thank
you.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: We had our first sight of  this Advanced Technology
Institute Bill on 10 September this year—not last. Three days later we had our first
reading, and in those 3 days we looked at the bill—as much as you can in a few days—
and, frankly, we saw no harm in it. We sa w no massive benefit, nor did we see a great
deal of harm. We thought there was a possibility  that this proposed new entity might do
some good, and so we supported the bill through to the Education and Science
Committee.
We entirely agree that it is important that  we seek to maintain and increase the
strength of the direct links between science and research and actual commercial activity.
We are very much in favour of a cleantech, greentech economy. That is the way of the
21st century, unlike some of the Government’s  policies, which are leaping backward
8 Nov 2012 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 6477
into the early 19th century. We see that this is an important and necessary thing to do—
to increase our output in the high-tech sector.
The question that has since come to us in  terms of the proposal to establish this
Advanced Technology Institute is quite a simple question. It is simply to ask why. What
is actually the need for such an organi sation? What gap does it fill? What is the
necessity for an entirely new entity, a new structure, rather than working within existing
structures and existing sets of relationshi ps, perhaps enhancing those and making them
work a little differently or better? What is so wrong with Industrial Research, the
institute that, to date, is effectively doing wh at this new entity is supposed to do? If one
has a look at the statement of intent for the current year to June 2013, the objectives, the
strategic goals, of our Indus trial Research are fundamenta lly the same as what is
proposed for this new Advanced Technology Institute, this new organisation.
I must say that it seems that this Government seems to have a very peculiar
relationship with the public sector. And I must say in passing that I was equally
surprised and somewhat amused by the chai r of the committee, Nikki Kaye, launching
into the Labour Party for daring to suggest that the unions might be represented on the
board of this entity. The representatives of the scientists, the technicians, the
tradespeople who actually design and make stuff—how dare Labour propose that they
should be represented on a body that will make key decisions about linking the science
and the economic and social outcomes!
More particularly, this Govern ment seems to have a perverse situation. It is putting
the boot into the public sector. In  the name of so-called effici encies it is actually taking
away the capacity of the public sector to  do its job, and yet when the Government
perceives a problem, it tends to create a new ent ity, a new public sector entity. It did it
with the Productivity Commission. Ackno wledging that we have a very low
productivity economy, the Government said “Let’s create a public entity to try to solve
it.”, which, to date, has clearly failed to a ddress even the key issues, let alone resolve
them. Similarly with this bill, we have an issue about not getting enough high-tech,
high-value manufacturing, so let us cr eate a new public organisation, a new
bureaucracy. Perhaps that will do the trick. It is a very peculiar response from a
Government that alleges that it represents the private sector rather than the public sector.
We received submissions on the Advanced Technology Institute proposal, on the bill.
There were not that many of them, and clea rly they were written in haste, because
submitters were given, really, only days, never mind weeks, to come up with and
prepare them. Nevertheless, they were of ve ry good quality. They were from some very
significant commentators, some important players in the sector, and they all offered—
with one or two notable exceptions—very quali fied support, and I do stress the word
“qualified”. Everybody agrees, as the Greens did at the first reading, that an entity, some
sort of a networking organisation that can bring together our science and research
capacity with our good business brains and our good business organisations, is a good
thing. But the qualifications came through a nd they tended to follow themes—common
issues that came through again and again fr om the various submitters. These included
the likelihood that this ne w organisation would duplicate and even disrupt existing
successful and productive rela tionships and situations th at already exist with the
commercialisation arms of the universities and the members of the economic
development agencies that have done some very solid and robust work over a number of
years in this area.
The committee did agree, on prompting from , particularly, Labour and the Greens,
that clause 14 of the bill s hould include the word “collabor ate”, just to drive home the
fact that this organisation, the new Adva nced Technology Institute, should demand that
we get a high level of collaboration rather th an a more top-down hi erarchical approach.
6478 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 8 Nov 2012
That was a good step. It was a positive step, and we supported that. It was a necessary
step, but it was not a sufficient one in te rms of endeavouring to avoid the almost
inevitability of duplication and disruption of what are currently well-functioning and
very productive relationships.
The world has not been sitting idly by, waiting for this Government to create an
entity that will bridge the gap, if you like, or will strengthen the relationships between
research, science, and technology—that cr eative sector—and the business sector. Of
course, business done well is also a creative activ ity. Again, as I say, we absolutely
support the principle of doing th at, but there has been a great deal of very good work
done over a number of years. Nowhere in this  bill—it is so loosely drafted; it is so
poorly supported by argument—do we see any reassurance that the institute will not
come in with size 11 boots and trample all over, disrupt, and set back a lot of those very
positive relationships that already exist. One hopes that the Minister of Science and
Innovation is even aware of them and that he has considered that, but there is no
evidence of that having happened. We asked the obvious question of the committee
about what the nature would be of the re lationships between the Advanced Technology
Institute and these other incubators—the commercialisation arms and so on. The answer
we got was that no decisions had yet been made about how those relationships will be
maintained or held. What an entirely unhelpful response that was.
The extent to which the Advanced Technol ogy Institute would become a provider of
science and therefore a competitor to the other organisations was also of concern to
many of the submitters. Again, I hope nobody will raise the imaginary objection of self-
interest. These are senior respected scie ntists and commentators who are actually
looking at what is good for this country—what is good in terms of achieving the
proposed goals of this legisla tion. The dean of science at Auckland University gave the
committee a supplementary submission. He wa s very concerned th at the Advanced
Technology Institute should function in predom inantly a service role. He suggested that
the research function should be a very minor  component of the in stitute’s role and,
ideally, should occur only through the tran sition period. He went on to say that the
arguments that the Advanced Technology Instit ute requires a research  capacity to fill
the gaps that other institutions could not meet are not persuasive, and are based on a
limited understanding of research and the ch allenges of working with the high-value
manufacturing sector.
In regards to concerns about the Advanced Technology Institute being both a funding
agency and a provider of research, clause 13(1)(f) of the bill tells us simply that the
Advanced Technology Institute will allocate  and administer research, science, and
technology funding. The very obvious and logica l question for the select committee to
ask was what funding? How much? How mu ch control will it have over research
funding in New Zealand? Again, the respon se we got back from the Ministry of
Business, Innovation and Employment was that  no decisions had been made regarding
which funding the Advanced Technology Institu te will administer, because the ministry
is currently reviewing the schemes. A report back to Cabinet is due on 30 November, by
which time this bill, we expect, will be done  and dusted. We are be ing asked to support
a pig in a poke. We do not know what the boun daries of this organisation will be. We
do not know what its relationship will be with  existing, very positive initiatives. We do
not know what funding it will control. We suspect that it will be a lot.
The issue of funding would be less critical  if this was an organisation with any
autonomy. It is a Crown agent. It must give  effect to Government policy. It has very
little autonomy. This gives the Minister of the day licence to pick winners, and picking
winners was one of those activities that th e late, great Sir Paul Callaghan directly
advised us to avoid li ke the plague. He was absolutely clear on that point. Governments
8 Nov 2012 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 6479
are very bad at picking winners, and th e New Zealand Manufacturers and Exporters
Association, which has already been menti oned, in its opposition to this organisation
made it clear that picking winners has a dishono urable history of comp lete failure. It is
very hard to argue with that.
I have outlined some of the objections from submitters. I look forward to the
Committee stage and the third reading, when we will be able to engage a little more. For
the moment, on balance, the Greens, given all the flaws in this bill—we see that Labour
is supporting it and we respect its decision; we were on a bit of a tightrope as well—
cannot support an entity we know so little about, when the legislation is so poorly
drafted and where the intenti ons, the operational functions, the role, and the powers of
this entity are unknown. We will therefore not be supporting this legislation.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: It is a pleasure to ta ke a call in the second
reading of the Advanced Technology Institute B ill. In doing so, I just want to cover off
a couple of issues that other members have raised in their speeches. Effectively, of
interest is the submission from Business New Zealand, where it quoted that it firmly
advocates that the Advanced Technology Inst itute needs to have operational research
and development capability in order to have cr edibility and skin in the game. That is a
very relevant comment, because, when we look at it, what the Advanced Technology
Institute will be is a business-led, market-foc used research institute, and it needs to be
successful.
There has always been a gap in the market, and we have known for a long time that
we do need a business-focused re search institute. When you look at the genesis of this
bill, it came not only from a Government agenda of innovation and economic growth.
One has only to research the situation the genesis came from, and also the empowering
innovation conference. One has only to read that document to understand how in sync
with business this Government is. I just ha ve to make that point, because there is a
history of a gap in the market, and the Advanced Technology Institute is designed to fix
this.
There were those comments that were raised on the other side of the House of a lack
of accountability. For goodness’ sake, inside this bill it prescribes how that transparency
will be brought to this House. The Auditor-G eneral will annually audit the process. It
will be very transparent.
With regard to the argument from the othe r side of the House about the confusion
and confliction between the funder/ provider split, this is part of the efficiency that we
also saw when we brought together the New Zealand Transport Agency, which was
something Labour did. Some of the arguments that we are hearing are about a trip back
to the 19th century. This is a bill that has its day in the 21st century. I have great pleasure
in supporting the bill.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. I stand to speak on the
Advanced Technology Institute Bill. I would just like to remind the House that New
Zealand First was actually the only party that opposed this bill at its first reading, on the
grounds that this work was al ready being done. I am pleased to stand here and say that
we were right, and we were proven right by just about every submitter who came to see
us. We are very pleased with the work th at the Education and Science Committee has
done within very tight time frames. We w ould have liked to ha ve more opportunity
from the Government to really flesh this out and to have a greater input from the
industry itself, but the submissi ons we did get were valid, th ey were in-depth, and they
were well-thought-out, and I ap preciated the level of expe rtise that was brought by the
submitters to this topic in the very short time frame that we had.
There was a lot of work done around the word “collaboration”—a lot of work
done—and a lot of talk and discussion around  the role of the Advanced Technology
6480 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 8 Nov 2012
Institute and making sure that it did not dupl icate, that it did not compete with people
currently doing the research work and curr ently inside this environment. However,
those submitters who were doing this wor k, although they were very concerned that
another competitor was not put into the co ntestable research funding market and that
there was not a duplication of expense and a duplication of work done, did acknowledge
the need for an organisation that was aware of all the players in that area, so that people
could be connected. I think, if I recall correctly, one of the conversations we had at the
select committee was that 80 percent of the Advanced T echnology Institute’s role is
actually going to be about conne cting people. Eighty percent of  the institute’s role will
be about the relationship between business and the researchers, and bringing those
organisations together appropriately to take a product from a certain place and be able to
commercialise it.
I am going to take this oppor tunity, however, while the Hon David Carter is here, to
talk about the fact that there still is a bit of a gap here. I hope that the other 20 percent of
the institute’s role that we have talked  about—we do not know how much money will
be dedicated or what budget line  will be given to this 20 percent, which is the research
itself that the institute will be looking at undertaking, because that information is not
available to us yet. There is  a bit of a concern I still ha ve, when I hear the Hon David
Carter speaking and Colin King talking, that  we are still talking about widgets and
gadgets that have been produced, that this bill is just about looking at them, figuring out
a way to improve, and going on to commercialising that market. I see Mr King shaking
his head, and that is a good thing. I am pleased to see that. We have now got that in the
Hansard. That is great.
For example, on 30 October I was with th e Taipei cultural and commerce office
representative, the consul-gener al of Japan, and the deputy consul-general of Japan at
the Mahurangi Technical Institute in Warkworth. It has taken eggs from eels. It can take
2 million eel eggs, get 2 million live births, a nd keep those eels alive for 12 days, but it
now needs $3 million to take those eels from 12 days to mass production. That market,
if we can get that investme nt from this Government—I do not know whether it is
something the Advanced Technical Institute would be able to use part of that 20 percent
to invest in—is not yet commercialised. Should that industry be commercialised, should
that investment be made, it would be bigger than oyster farming and bigger than mussel
farming. That is an industry that this country could really lift off on.
But when we do not have an organisation that  can invest in that way, we leave those
people vulnerable to having to sell their intellectual property overseas, and that
intellectual property goes overs eas and it stays overseas. So  I am hoping that part of
what we are trying to create here is that the 20 percent that the institute will actually be
using for research investment will be invest ed in those sorts of areas, and will not—
definitely not—be used to compete with  other researchers and other business
organisations that are working well but just need linkages.
There was another point that New Zealand First tried to have—a s mentioned in our
minority report—and it was a very small thi ng. It was a single wo rd. It was a single
word that we were hoping to have inserted in to clause 14(1)(b). Clause 14(1) reads: “In
meeting its main objective, and performing its functions, ATI must—… (b) proactively
engage and collaborate with businesses, other RS&T provide rs, and other persons that
ATI considers relevant to the performance of its functions;”. All we asked for was the
word “identify”. We asked for the word “i dentify” to be inserted after the word
“proactively” and before the word “engage”,  so it would read “proactively identify,
engage and collaborate”. It may seem very sm all, but the point of inserting that word
was to ensure that one of the things the A dvanced Technology Institute must do is first
of all find out who is in the market, so that it can then go and engage and collaborate.
8 Nov 2012 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 6481
That word would take away the excuse, should it enter into competition with anybody
currently in the market, that it did not know they were there. It is a very small thing, but
a very practical thing to make  sure that people do know who is in that market, that the
institute does not enter into competition wi th people who are providing this service
already.
There is another little concern that I have . I voiced it at the time. It is around the
FoodBowl of Auckland. The FoodBowl is going  to be absorbed—that may not be the
appropriate word. It is going to become part of the Adva nced Technology Institute. The
FoodBowl was partially funded by the ratepayers of Auck land, and it is about to be
absorbed. I would suggest that there is some compensation that needs to be paid to the
ratepayers of Auckland for losing this asset.  If the Government benches would like to
know the amount of money that has been inve sted by the ratepayers of Auckland in the
FoodBowl, then they can contact my office and I will have that amount sent to them.
We opposed this bill to start with. New Zealand First will now be supporting this bill.
We support it because we have been listened to. The submitters have supported our
original concerns around th is bill. We believe that the work done by the select
committee was adequate and strong for the time frame it was given. We will be
watching the institute to see that it does not compete for contestable funding. We will be
seeking support for the Mahurangi Technical Institute and the eel project, and if there is
anything extra, there is a whitebait project th ere that could actually do with a bit of an
input, as well. Just in clos ing, we would like to thank all members of the select
committee for what was a collaborative process. We will be supporting this bill.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise in support of
the second reading of this Advanced Technology Institute Bill. I would like to join with
previous speakers in acknowledging how appropr iate it is that the institute will be
named after the late Sir Paul Callaghan. I think that naming the institute after such a
distinguished New Zealander gives weight to  the very appropriate  benefits that the
institute will provide for us as a nation. It  is all about good ideas, good initiatives, and
good inventions being collaborated with rese arch and put together to get good products
to market faster, so that we can grow our ec onomy and so that the real benefits for New
Zealand will be constructively turned into something positive, tangible, and real.
I too would like to acknowledge the good work of the Education and Science
Committee. Under the very capable chairmansh ip of Nikki Kaye, I thought the select
committee worked diligently and promptly through a tight time frame. I want to
particularly acknowledge the co ntribution of the previous New Zealand First speaker,
Tracey Martin. As she rightly said, her part y started off opposing th is legislation, but
because of the collaborative approach and the sensible, intelligent, and dignified way
that the committee conduc ted its affairs, we were able  to come to, I think, a very
workable conclusion. So I think, for me, this  process has helped demonstrate the very
effective nature of the entire select comm ittee process, even when working under tight
time constraints. I want to acknowledge that.
There were a number of very good submissi ons. In fact, the committee received 23
excellent submissions, I thought. Seven subm itters appeared before the committee and
gave oral presentations. The vast majority of those were in favour of the bill. I think that
when we heard the submissions we were able to  get a real insight into the potential that
exists in the marketplace for this collabora tion of ideas, wit, and imagination when put
together with research, and the potential for great things that can come when those two
are put together and come out at the other end of the exercise producing not just widgets
but eels, possibly whitebait, and a whole range  of other things. I am looking forward to
the whitebait-tasting sessions. I am a person who has come from a business background.
I now find myself as an MP finding as I trip around the very beautiful Coromandel
6482 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 8 Nov 2012
electorate that not only do we have a wonderful environment but we have these
remarkably innovative people who have terrifically good ideas.
I think that the Advanced Technology Institute set-up and establishment will provide
a terrific opportunity for those people to work with some really smart research
development people and bring to gether terrific ideas. So I commend this bill to the
House. I am looking forward to the Committee stage and to progressing it to its final
conclusion.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: I rise to support the second reading of the Advanced
Technology Institute Bill, but it is lukewarm support, as yo u have already heard from
Labour speakers before me, because, effectivel y, unfortunately, this  is an opportunity
gone begging. It is another example from this Government of too little, too late—far too
little, far too late. Today we have hear d the unwelcome news—the shocking news,
actually—that unemployment has increased ag ain to 7.3 percent. The Government
would have us believe that it has got a pl an. Apparently, we are hearing through this
debate today, there is an economic plan. Well,  if there is a plan, it is not working. And
when that was put to Bill Engl ish earlier this week he said  that its economic plan is
working. That is what he informed the House. Well, that economic plan, if it is working,
must be a plan to have high unemployment and low wages, because that is, in fact,
exactly what is happening in New Zealand, and that is why we need a much better
response than this bill from this Government.
Although I guess it sounds like the Governme nt is doing something—it is going to
create a new Crown entity. That is what it is going to do. That is going to fix the
problems in New Zealand! Go and create a ne w Crown entity. That is exactly what this
bill is doing. There is high unemployment and low wages, and what does the National
Government do? It goes and establishes a new Crown entity. And in that new Crown
entity the Government clearly has no interest in what workers have to contribute to the
innovation of this country. During this debate it was very sad to hear the chair of the
Education and Science Committ ee, Nikki Kaye, use her—oh, she did not use even 10
minutes; I think she might have used 5 minut es, because there is not too much to say
about this bill. It does not do too much. She us ed most of that time to attack the Labour
Party for daring to say that workers should have a say in this Crown entity, and that
workers have something to contribute to  innovation. Has that Government learnt
nothing from the Pike River mine  disaster? Has it learnt nothing from the events of this
week and the report that landed on its desk  about the importance of involving workers
in big decisions? Has it learnt nothing? Nikki Kaye used this debate to attack the Labour
Party for insisting that work ers do have a right to have something to say about their
future, and that workers do have someth ing to contribute about innovation. They
certainly have a lot more than that Govern ment has to contribute to the discussion of
innovation. If this is the best  that the Government can co me up with, it is woefully—
woefully—inadequate.
I too want to acknowledge and honour the memory—honour the memory—of Sir
Paul Callaghan, but this bill does not honour his memory. This establishment of an
Advanced Technology Institute falls woefully  short—woefully short—of the sort of
vision that Sir Paul Callagha n had for a proper investment in innovation in science. He
had a vision of a high-wage economy, not the low-wage economy that that Government
is investing in and continuing to argue for in this House by saying that unions have no
role in innovation. For goodness’ sake! Read the Pike River mine report. Understand the
importance of working people and their co ntribution to the economy. Understand how
important it is that we get it right for this country. We will not get it right if working
people are not invested in and engaged in and part of that decision-making process. This
bill demonstrates again how little faith—how  little faith—the Government has in
8 Nov 2012 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 6483
working people, how little it values their co ntribution to the economy. It is another
example of exactly that.
I have a real concern about the process fo r this bill because it was entirely rushed. I
can think only that the Minist er of Science and Innovation di d not have his act together
with regards to this bill, because suddenl y, without any notice to the Education and
Science Committee—and this is a select committee I sit on—there was a bill put on us
that apparently we had to deal with in a ma tter of weeks. This is supposed to be a large
vision, the new vision for this Government that is going to save the country, and yet the
Education and Science Committee had to deal with it in a matter of weeks. Blink and
you would miss it, the process for this bill. In  fact, in my instance, go and hear a few
submissions on paid parental leave and you miss it. I actually was not able to participate
in hearing any of the submissions on this bill, because it was so truncated—so
truncated. If this is the thing that is goi ng to turn round the New Zealand economy, if
this is the big hope that this Government is going to give those several thousand newly
unemployed people in New Zealand whom we ha ve learnt about today, then it deserved
to have more attention paid to it. It deserv ed to have a Minister who at least could get
the bill in a form where it could be presente d to the House for first reading so that a
select committee could have a reasonable am ount of time to actually deliberate on it.
The select committee did not have adequate time to deliberate on it. It was not given
due regard, and if that rushed  process is an example of how  the National Party wants to
honour one of our very finest scientists, then I am afraid it does fall woefully short. I
hope that I can be proven wrong and I hope that this Crown entity does live up to his
vision, but there is nothing in the bill that w ould convince me that that, in fact, will be
the case.
The Government does not want  to address the really big issues when it comes to
research and development. It will not —despite now overwhelming expert advice—
consider returning the research and developm ent tax credits that it slashed, that this
Government actually dumped. Research a nd development tax credits were warmly
welcomed by business, were warmly welcomed by the science fraternity, as being a
really significant way, not like this bill, that we could act ually make a great deal of
difference and improvement in the investment  in research and development in this
country. That is the type of very specific and detailed policy that would make a tangible
difference to research and development and innovation in this country. Will the
Government go near that? Will it even en tertain the idea? Worse than not even
entertaining the idea, it got rid of it.
When the Government got rid of that policy, it got rid of a significant opportunity to
improve this country’s record when it comes to research and development. Ever since it
got rid of it, it has been scrambling to try to find a replacement. As we have heard from
a previous speaker, the voucher system has not replaced it. That has been a failure. Now
it is trying to say that the development of  a Crown entity will somehow replace that
very good Labour policy of a research and development tax credit. Well, it plainly will
not. This is woefully inadequate and I challenge the Government to actually come up
with something that will work. We do not need any more slogans like a cycleway. That
failed as well. A Crown entity is another at tempt to make it look like the Government is
doing something. But we will support it because, quite frankly, doing something, no
matter how little, is better than  doing nothing at all, which is what the Government has
been doing to date.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): Exhausting—absolutely exhausting.
The Advanced Technology Institu te Bill is a positive bill. Ther e has been a little bit of
focus, actually, on what was seen as a truncated  or a supposedly fast process. I actually
think the process was sufficient.
6484 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 8 Nov 2012
Those of us who do research in different forms know that you come across a eureka
moment, and it can come at any point in time.  I think this Government realised fairly
early on the eureka moment around the Advanced  Technology Institute Bill. This is an
opportunity for the country, and one that s hould be embraced enthusiastically. I think
that when we look at the majority of the 23 submissions that we got in the Education
and Science Committee, people were behind this. There are always, I suppose, some
cosmetic or small aspects to be discussed, but by and large people are supportive of this
project. This Government is keen to get on with the job—that is the key.
When we look at the Advanced Technology In stitute Bill, there have been a number
of distractions today in the speeches around it,  but there really are two words that sum
up the bill. The first is “mechanism”, and the second is “conduit”. This is a mechanism,
a legislative mechanism, to bring about a body to facilitate research and development in
New Zealand. It is a mechanism. It does not n eed to be incredibly prescriptive. It does
not need to reflect ideology. It does not need to say which mates have to be on the
boards. This is a mechanism, a legislativ e mechanism to bring about an Advanced
Technology Institute.
What is this institute about? It is a conduit.  At the end of the day, it is about taking
the best research in New Zealand and acting as  a conduit to make the research into a
commercially viable option. It mirrors a lot of institutes around the world. I can think of
one that is somewhat similar. I had the pleasure earlier this year to go to the United
States to look at the American political syst em. One part of our trip was to go into
Massachusetts—it was actually back to a place, Cambridge, where I had lived—to see
the Cambridge Innovation Center. This is a place that acts as a conduit, taking good
ideas and linking them to business. One of  the most fascinating elements of the
Cambridge Innovation Center was that the likes  of Google and Microsoft had chosen to
build nearby it. It is acting as a conduit—ag ain, facilitating research, development, and
good ideas supportively and actua lly linking them across to business. I think when I
look at the Advanced Technology Institute, ther e are degrees and direct similarities at
work there.
Again, it is important to see that this bill is, firstly, a mechanism and, secondly, a
conduit. It is not something to be distract ed, pulled apart, and seen as sort of a
facilitation of cronyism, or what ever else has been thrown at  it today. This is a conduit
for the substantial funding that the Government does put into research and development.
There is often talk about these tax credits and so forth, but what is often forgotten is that
this Government has successively increa sed the total funding into research and
development. As part of Budget 2012 this  Government has allocated approximately
$166 million over 4 years to the Advanced Technology Institute—$166 million over 4
years. This is a substantial contribution by the Government to support people in New
Zealand.
In fact, it also touches on, and gets very similar to, something we have already out by
Auckland Airport. There is a facility there to act as a conduit around the food industry, a
place where people come with their ideas and their research, if you like, and turn them
into something that is commercially viable. Again, there are really good examples, both
local and overseas, that this Advanced Technology Institute Bill is working on.
So I think it is really important that we do not get distracted by the cronyistic designs
of some parties. It is certainly not a place to  fall into the Chicken Little argument that
this is going to be the end of research in New Zealand—we have heard that today. This
is a bill, a legislative mechanism—[ Interruption]; indeed—to facilitate and help people
bring that cutting-edge research that New Z ealand has. We think about the work that
Orion Health does, we think of the work that Fisher and Paykel Healthcare does. I think,
actually, of a few of my friends who work within the scientific area. They want this bill.
8 Nov 2012 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 6485
They are already at the coalface doing fa ntastic work. Let us get on with it. We
promptly looked at the bill. We appropriately  looked at the bill. Let us get it on to the
Committee and the third reading.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Dr David Clark—a 10-minute call.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: There has been under-investment
by National in research and development—less than 1 percent of GDP, compared with
Denmark and Finland with about 3 to 4 percent of GDP. We know the OECD average is
around 2.5 percent. This woef ul under-investment in res earch and development is
something this Government is doing nothing to  address. National ch ose, of course, to
cut the research and developm ent tax credits that Labour put  in place and it has also
slashed budgets in other areas. It goes to show that those members just do not get it.
You know, they just do not get it. There are so me issues they just do not get. There is
also a woeful under-investment in private se ctor research and development, which is
linked to the public sector re search and development investment, as is shown across the
OECD. The bureaucratic subsidy approach th at National favours does not even fit with
its language of having a busines s-friendly, business-led approach. It is unfortunate; that
is all you can say about it—a whole lot of red tape, a slow way of doing business, and it
does not really encourage those who are the i nnovators in our society, who want to take
it forward, and who want to make sure that  there are high-payi ng, high-skilled, high-
tech manufacturing jobs for the future ahead of us.
We saw with the emissions trading legislation that we debated just before this
Advanced Technology Institute Bill that inst ead, the Government is preoccupying itself
with taking the country backwards by extending subsidies for the businesses that are not
in the high-tech space. That paints a picture of a Governme nt that has its eye off the
ball, that does not have a plan for this country—

items.speaker: Michael Woodhouse
items.text: Are they sunset industries, too?

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: —for taking our industries forward. Mr Woodhouse, the
member opposite, is talking about sunset indus tries. No doubt he is including in there
Hillside in Dunedin. Fisher and Paykel, pr obably, which shut down its manufacturing,
would be a sunset industry to Mr Woodhouse, I suspect. He does not care that the jobs
are going in Dunedin. He does not care that Tamahine Apparel Solutions shut down. He
does not care that the jobs went at Delta Utility Servi ces. He does not care that the
Inland Revenue Department is shutting down its local services, or that the taxpayer
money that goes into Dunedin is being taken out so that there is an increase in
unemployment locally. These are foolish th ings to argue, Mr Woodhouse. The local
situation in Dunedin is dire and the unemployment levels are rising, and it is because of
policies like this one we see before us, whic h really is not favourable to businesses that
want to innovate, but instead makes it more complicated.
It would be a good thing as part of a wider p ackage, and it is a timid step in the right
direction. So, ultimately, although it is a slight ly bitter pill, Labour will be supporting
this legislation because we think this ki nd of thing can be built on—if we did have
decent research and development credits, if we had some joined-up policy, if we had
decent procurement policies, if we took care of  the bigger picture, if we looked at the
kind of macro-prudential tools that the Rese rve Bank might need to ensure that we
actually had jobs and a thriving economy and an exchange rate that was favourable to
our manufacturing export sector, if we had pr o-growth tax policy, if we had the likes of
a capital gains tax that would see money flow ing from the speculative sector toward the
productive sector, and if we had procurement policies that actually looked at the whole
economy.
When the Hillside trains were to be built , if we had looked at the wider economic
benefit, it might have been a very different equation. If we had looked at the tax paid by
6486 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 8 Nov 2012
those people who were doing the manufacturing,  who had the jobs, and if we looked at
the money going to those industries that provide work into Hillside and the other
engineering firms, and if we looked at the wider benefits to our country of having a
capable manufacturing sector, we might have  had a different outcome. So the research
and development tax policies, of course, are critical in this context, but those other
things cannot be ignored, because they ar e about ensuring that we do have economic
development in New Zealand.
To come back to that point, John Ke y did promise 170,000 new jobs, and today, just
today, we have the highest jobless rate in 13 ye ars. It is the highest jobless rate in 13
years. There are 175,000 people looking for wor k. It has not been this bad since Bill
English was last finance Minister in the 1990s . Things have not been this bad. The only
common element, I guess, we can see there very plainly. This timid approach to
innovation, which sees this under-investment, is part of a bigger picture, and it is also,
in some ways, explained by the way this bill has been put through. We in the Labour
Party believe that if you want  to get good policy that supp orts industry, that supports
commercialisation, that supports the scientif ic community, and that actually builds our
economy, you need proper input from industry. You actually have to be willing to listen
to the businesses that are doing this stuff, not ramming it through at high speed, not
putting it through a “blink and you miss it” select committee process.
You need to be looking at that bigger picture, of course—t he overvalued currency
and the tools that would address that—and the other things that are going on in the New
Zealand sector that are leading to the job lo sses that this Government has overseen, the
current decline in the economy, and the drop in real wages. Recently announced was the
median wage drop of 3 percent. Those things all need to be taken into account when you
are setting the policy. But this process has not helped. Speeding th is through the select
committee does not give industry, the scie ntific community, economic development
communities, and members of the public the op portunity to make the contributions they
can make that would actually make sure that we had proper, decent policy in this area.
Even if the Government does not have a vision for it, that select committee process is an
opportunity to get input from those that do.
The high-tech manufacturing sector, job sk ills, and so on should also be given an
explicit focus in this bill. This is what one of the submitters—one of the few submitters
who was allowed to come along in the time fr ame, or was able to—pointed to, and we
support this. Those objectives of having a hi gh-tech manufacturing sector for increasing
jobs and increasing skills shoul d be given an explicit focus in  the bill. Why not make it
clear that that is what we are trying to achie ve with this? Then questions can be asked if
it is not being achieved, so that we can actually have accountability measures and a
clear focus. Likewise, in the purpose st atement, it would be great—it would be
crucial—that there not be unnecessary dupli cation and competition with pre-existing
research provision by the Advanced Technology Institute. Why not make that explicit in
the legislation? Again, there were some submitters who were able to make the tightened
time frame who made that point, and Labour ag rees with that. There are sensible and
serious things that could have been in cluded to improve the economic prospects
associated with this initiative that were not taken into account.
Another aspect, another conflict, that sits in this bill is the funder/provider split. This
is something that fits into basic pub lic sector management principles. The
funder/provider split is something you can ask Treasury about.  It will wax lyrical about
the importance of making sure that there is not a conflict between those who are bidding
into the process and those who have got th e funding. So that exists with the active
functions of the Advanced Technology Instit ute: the research and development, the
knowledge and technology transfer functions , and the enabling functions—the funding
8 Nov 2012 Advanced Technology Institute Bill 6487
to third parties. We also note that there were very few submissions from industry and
businesses directly engaged in  high-value manufacturing, and that has got to be a
concern.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: They hardly had time to do it.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: Well, they did not have time to do it, as my colleague the Hon
Trevor Mallard points out. That means that we  are likely to get flawed legislation and
that we are not going to get legislation that  could be achieving to the extent that is
possible if the proper processes of this Parliament are observed, along with the habits of
good parliamentary conduct. Labour also thinks that the education sector could be quite
directly tied in so that, again, the advice a nd so on that is coming in takes account of
that wider context. These are all things that were overlooked.
On its own, the Advanced Technology Inst itute cannot successfully transform our
economy. It could be better, but overall it fits within a wider context where the
Government has its eye off the ball, does not have a plan, and is not taking care of those
bigger-picture issues, such as the exchange rate, which makes it very difficult for the
manufacturing sector. That is why we ar e seeing those engaged in the manufacturing
sector drop off—the lowest numbers since stat istics began, we learnt yesterday. That is
why if you do not pay attenti on to those things, if you do not have pro-growth tax
policies that support industries, if you do not have simplified business practices, if you
are not actually looking out and listening to what is going on more  broadly, and if you
are not willing to make the bi g changes to get our economy back on track, it will not
happen. This Government does not have a plan. It is overseeing the worst economic
record of any Government in 50 years. It potters along. It is not  making a difference,
and I look forward to hearing what Mr Woodhouse has to say about how this is going to
be turned round, because there is no evidence it is in the current settings.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: It is my great pleasure  to take the last call
in the second reading debate on the Advan ced Technology Institute Bill. I want to make
a couple of comments based on submissions  from previous speakers. I start by
acknowledging Tracey Martin and the New Zeala nd First Party for, firstly, what was a
very thoughtful contribution to this debate , but also for the fact that having voted
against this bill at its first reading, the New Zealand First Party has considered and
changed that position. I think that is a merit of the maturity of the thought that has gone
into it. Also, my colleagues on the Education and Science Committee have
acknowledged the contribution Ms Martin is making to that committee.
I want to congratulate Sue Moroney and Dr David Clark on and thank them for their
continued support of a research  and development tax credit. I do so on behalf of my
colleagues in the Institute of Chartered Accountants of New Zealand, because it will be
they who benefit the most from that ph ilosophically flawed goal. Please keep
campaigning on it. If that is all Labour has to innovate in this country, then that is fine
by us.
The last thing I would say is to Dr David Clark. I do not have th e luxury of focusing
on just the negative things that are happe ning in Dunedin—and Hillside is a very
concerning thing. It is my duty, my obligati on, and a challenge to point out the positive
things. So for the New Zealand Honey C o., AbacusBio, Farra Engineering, Cowell’s
Genuine Pavlova, Pacific Edge  Biotechnology, Separett, Silver  Fern Farms, Fonterra,
Speights Brewery, for the many small compan ies that are benefiting from record
numbers of cruise ship visits into Dunedi n and the oil and gas exploration opportunities
that present a massive manufacturing opportunity, I will stand up, I will fly the flag, and
I will say that the policies of this Government and this bill will benefit Dunedin.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. Is it appropriate for the member to refer to “you” in that way?

items.text: We have ruled on that several times. The debate has now
